final_proof:
We use the following classical consequence of Ingham's theorem on gaps between consecutive primes.

**Short-interval prime theorem.** There are constants \(C>0\) and \(x_0>0\) such that, for every real \(x\ge x_0\), there is a prime \(q\) satisfying
\[
x<q<x+C x^{5/8}.
\]
Indeed, Ingham's prime-gap theorem says that the gap from a sufficiently large prime \(r\) to its successor is at most \(C r^{5/8}\), after choosing a suitable constant \(C\). Given sufficiently large \(x\), take the greatest prime \(r\le x\) and let \(q\) be its successor. Then \(q>x\) and
\[
q-x\le q-r\le C r^{5/8}\le Cx^{5/8},
\]
which proves the displayed form.

Choose an integer \(P\) so large that \(P^3\ge x_0\) and, for every integer \(p\ge P\),
\[
C p^{15/8}<3p^2+3p. \tag{1}
\]
Such a \(P\) exists because
\[
\frac{3p^2+3p}{p^{15/8}}=3p^{1/8}+3p^{-7/8}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Choose a prime \(p_1\ge P\). Having chosen a prime \(p_n\ge P\), apply the short-interval theorem with \(x=p_n^3\) and choose a prime \(p_{n+1}\) such that
\[
p_n^3<p_{n+1}<p_n^3+C p_n^{15/8}<(p_n+1)^3-1, \tag{2}
\]
where the last inequality follows from (1), since
\[
(p_n+1)^3-1=p_n^3+3p_n^2+3p_n.
\]
In particular, \(p_{n+1}>p_n\ge P\), so this construction continues indefinitely.

For \(n\ge1\), set
\[
a_n=p_n^{1/3^n},\qquad b_n=(p_n+1)^{1/3^n}.
\]
The left inequality in (2) gives \(a_{n+1}>a_n\). The right inequality gives
\[
p_{n+1}+1<(p_n+1)^3,
\]
and hence \(b_{n+1}<b_n\). It also gives \(a_{n+1}<b_n\). Inductively, therefore, \(a_m<b_n\) whenever \(m>n\). Thus \((a_n)\) is increasing and bounded above by \(b_1\), so it has a real limit. Define
\[
A=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n.
\]

Fix \(n\ge1\). Since \((a_m)\) is increasing and \(a_{n+1}>a_n\),
\[
A\ge a_{n+1}>a_n.
\]
On the other hand, \(a_m<b_{n+1}\) for every \(m>n+1\), so passing to the limit gives \(A\le b_{n+1}<b_n\). Consequently,
\[
p_n=a_n^{3^n}<A^{3^n}<b_n^{3^n}=p_n+1.
\]
It follows that \(\lfloor A^{3^n}\rfloor=p_n\), which is prime, for every positive integer \(n\). Therefore such a real number \(A\) exists.
